D012_m001.question:
I’ve had this fear for about a year and a half now—ever since I saw a performer in a full costume at this art festival. It was one of those big-headed characters, really exaggerated features, and I don’t know why, but something just snapped in me. Ever since then, I can’t be near anything like that—parades, theme parks, even cartoons in mascots’ clothing on my phone.  

When I see one, my chest tightens, my breath gets shallow, and I just… freeze. I can’t move. I stood still in the middle of the street once, just staring, while my friend had to pull me away. It’s embarrassing, especially since I’m supposed to be open-minded, you know? I’m an art student—I work with masks and imagery—but this thing, it’s like my body shuts down no matter how much I tell myself it’s not real.  

I avoid a lot now. Group shows, festivals, even some classes if I think there might be performance art involved. I’ve missed critiques, and my professor noticed. I feel stupid, but it’s not something I can just reason away. The fear is instant. And the freezing—that’s the worst part. I’m trapped in my own skin until it passes.
D012_m001.options:
A. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Specific Phobia
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012_m002.question:
I’ve been feeling this way for about a year and a half now—maybe longer, but that’s when it started really affecting my life. I run a small bakery downtown, and I’m used to being on my feet all day, managing orders, working the counter. But lately, I’ve been avoiding things I never thought twice about before. The elevator in our building broke again last winter, and I had to take the freight elevator to bring up supplies… that’s when it first hit. My heart just started pounding, like it was going to burst, I couldn’t catch my breath, started sweating even though it was cold, and my hands were shaking so bad I dropped a tray of muffins.

Since then, I can’t do elevators. Not even the new one. And it’s spreading—now I get nervous going over the bridge to deliver croissants to the café on the other side. Just thinking about being stuck, enclosed, or high up with no way out… it makes my chest tighten. I take the stairs, even though it’s three flights, and I drive way out of the way to avoid tunnels. My daughter keeps asking me to visit her in Chicago, but flying? I can’t even consider it. I’ll take the train if I have to, no matter how long it takes.
D012_m002.options:
A. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Specific Phobia
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012_m003.question:
I’ve always loved being outdoors, but for the past year and a half, something’s shifted—especially when it comes to storms. It started after a bad thunderstorm woke me up one night, and since then, I can’t seem to shake this overwhelming dread when the sky darkens. I work long hours at the lab, and now I stress about getting caught in the rain or being alone in my apartment when a storm hits. 

When I see heavy clouds rolling in or hear thunder, my heart starts racing—like it’s going to burst. I get short of breath, start sweating even if it’s cold, and my hands shake so badly I can’t hold my coffee. Once, I had to leave the library during a downpour and ended up hyperventilating under the awning, too afraid to dash to my car. 

Logically, I know storms aren’t dangerous where I live—flooding’s rare, and buildings are safe. But my body doesn’t listen. I’ve started checking weather apps obsessively, and if rain’s forecasted, I cancel plans, stay late at the lab, or just feel on edge all day. It’s affecting my focus on my dissertation, and I hate feeling controlled by the sky.
D012_m003.options:
A. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Specific Phobia
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012_m004.question:
I’ve been the keeper out at Greyrock Lighthouse for about six years now—just me, the foghorn, and the sea. It’s quiet, which is why I took the job. After my mother passed, I needed space. But for the past year and a half, something’s been getting worse.  

It started small—just a tightness in my chest when I saw one of those old, weathered Halloween masks people sometimes leave in storage lockers. I don’t know why it stuck with me. But now, even the *thought* of a mask, especially ones with wide grins or hollow eyes, sends me into a kind of freeze. My heart hammers so hard I think I’m having a heart attack. I can’t breathe. Once, during a supply drop, a worker opened a crate with a rubber clown mask wrapped in newspaper—just for a joke, I guess—and I dropped to my knees. Couldn’t move for ten minutes.  

I’ve never liked them, but it wasn’t always like this. Now I check every package, every drawer, even the shadows in the lantern room, convinced I’ll see those blank, grinning faces staring back. I avoid the old keeper’s logs because someone pasted a picture of a parade float in one. I can’t have anyone visit with costumes, not even joking around. It’s not the dark. It’s not the isolation. It’s *that*—the masks. They feel… alive. And I can’t control it.
D012_m004.options:
A. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Specific Phobia
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012_m005.question:
I’ve been driving the underground line for nearly twenty years—same routine, same tunnels. But about a year and a half ago, something changed. It started when I saw a rat dart across the tracks just as I was pulling into the station. I didn’t think much of it at first—we all see them down there—but then, a few weeks later, I saw one near the service ladder during a safety check. That’s when it hit me. I froze. Just… couldn’t move. My hands locked up, like my body forgot how to work. I had to wait for a signal operator to call control to check on me.

Since then, it’s gotten worse. Just the thought of seeing a rat—or any rodent—on the tracks or in the tunnels makes my chest tighten. I keep imagining them crawling into the cab, coming up through the grates. My wife says it’s irrational—she doesn’t get it. I never used to care, but now I check the floor before I step on the platform. I’ve even started calling in sick a few times, just not wanting to go down there. I love my job, but I can’t shake this fear. It’s like I’m trapped in my own mind every time I clock in.
D012_m005.options:
A. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Specific Phobia
    D. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder

D012_m006.question:
I’ve always loved my job—being around books, helping people find information, the quiet rhythm of the library. But for the past year and a bit, something’s gotten worse: I can’t stand being in enclosed spaces. It started with the elevator at work. Even though I have an office on the second floor, I now take the stairs every single day, no matter how tired I am. If I have to go upstairs, I start feeling my heart race halfway up, like it’s going to burst. My hands sweat, I can’t catch my breath—it feels like the walls are closing in.

I’ve avoided going to events in buildings with small rooms, even book talks I used to love. Once, a friend made me go to a reading in the basement of a bookstore. I only made it through because she held my hand the whole time. I keep a small notebook in my pocket now—something tangible to focus on—otherwise, I feel like I’ll pass out.

I’m embarrassed, especially since I live alone and don’t have anyone to rely on regularly. It’s affecting my work. I turned down a promotion that would’ve meant more off-site meetings. It’s like I’m shrinking my world smaller and smaller, and I don’t know how much longer I can keep doing this.
D012_m006.options:
A. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    B. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    C. Specific Phobia
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D012_m007.question: I’ve been dreading this for over a year now—probably closer to thirteen months. It started gradually, but now just thinking about having to get on an airplane or ride up in one of those glass elevators makes my chest tighten and my hands sweat. I mean, I run a business; we have clients across the country. I should be out there meeting them, growing the company, but I can’t. I had to turn down a major partnership in Chicago because it meant flying. We ended up doing everything over video calls, which wasn’t the same. My wife keeps saying I need help—I cancel family trips, won’t even take the elevator at the hotel when we visit our daughter in New York. I take the stairs, no matter how many floors. I know it sounds extreme, but the thought of being trapped, especially up high or in a closed space with no way out… it just flips a switch in me. I feel like I’m going to pass out or start gasping in front of everyone. I’ve restructured my entire schedule around avoiding these situations. It’s affecting my work, my family time—everything. And the worst part? I can’t even explain it to people without sounding irrational. I just feel… stuck.
D012_m007.options:
A. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    B. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    C. Specific Phobia
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D012_m008.question:
I’ve always been uncomfortable around animals, but over the past year and a bit, it’s just gotten out of control—especially with dogs. It doesn’t matter if they’re small, on a leash, or even behind a window. The second I see one, my chest tightens, my heart starts racing, and I feel like I can’t breathe. Once, there was a dog in the lobby of my office building—just sitting there with its owner—and I couldn’t go in. I stood outside for 20 minutes, feeling ridiculous but completely frozen, until someone finally texted me that it was gone.

I work in IT auditing, so most of my job is at a desk, but I have to visit client sites occasionally, and now I panic before every trip. I check Google Street View to make sure there aren’t dogs in the yard or common areas. I’ve started declining assignments in residential neighborhoods. My manager doesn’t know why—I just say I’m not available.

I live alone, and that’s partly by design. I avoid walking in parks, won’t visit friends with pets, and even turned down a date because he mentioned he had a dog. It’s limiting, I know, but the thought of getting that close to one again… I can’t take the chance.
D012_m008.options:
A. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    B. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    C. Specific Phobia
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D012_m009.question:
I’ve always considered myself a rational person—I teach philosophy, so logic is kind of my thing. But for over a year now, I can’t even explain this… reaction I have to spiders. Not even big ones. Just *seeing* one, or sometimes just a smudge on the wall that looks like one, and my chest tightens, my heart explodes, I feel like I’m going to pass out or throw up. It’s instant. Like a switch. Once, during a lecture, a student flicked an eraser across the board and I thought it was a spider—I actually stopped mid-sentence, couldn’t breathe. Humiliating.  

I know they’re mostly harmless. I *know* that. But I can’t walk through my own garage anymore unless my wife checks it first. I avoid hiking, won’t visit friends with sheds or gardens. Last month I skipped a conference in Vermont because it was in an old lodge. What kind of academic refuses a keynote over *bugs*? But the dread… it’s paralyzing.  

My wife says I’ve changed. I don’t sit outside in the summer, I check the bed rigorously every night. I’ve even thought about early retirement because the campus greenhouse and biology wing—places I used to walk through all the time—are now off-limits. It’s not like me to avoid things. But this feels beyond control.
D012_m009.options:
A. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    B. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    C. Specific Phobia
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D012_m010.question:
I’ve been struggling with this fear for over a year now—ever since that thunderstorm last summer, the one where the power went out and the wind nearly ripped the roof off. Since then, I can’t seem to handle storms. When the sky darkens or the wind picks up, my chest tightens, my heart races, and I start sweating like I’m back in that moment. My wife says I look pale, almost frozen.  

Even thinking about a storm coming—like when the weatherman mentions a chance of thunder—sets me on edge. I check the forecast three or four times a day, just waiting for bad news. It’s exhausting. I used to enjoy sitting on the porch in the evenings, but now I stay inside once the sun goes down. I just don’t trust the dark the way I used to.  

The only time I’ll go out during storm season is if my wife is with me. Just knowing she’s beside me helps—like she’s my anchor. If she weren’t there, I don’t think I could do it. It’s not like me, you know? I spent thirty years managing city departments—kept calm during budget crises, floods, you name it. But this… this feels different. Like something’s taken hold and won’t let go. It's starting to feel like I’m not in control of my own life anymore.
D012_m010.options:
A. Persistent Depressive Disorder
    B. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    C. Specific Phobia
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D012_m011.question:
I’ve had this fear for over two years now—about two years and a month, actually. It started kind of suddenly, I guess. I’m terrified of spiders. Not just a little uneasy—like full-on panic. If I see one, even a tiny one, my chest tightens, I start shaking, and I can’t breathe right. Once, I saw one in the bathroom at work and had to leave the floor. My manager wasn’t happy.

Since it got worse, I’ve changed almost everything. I won’t go into the basement at home, even if my husband asks. We keep putting off laundry because of it. I won’t go camping or hiking—my husband and I used to do that sometimes, but now I make excuses. Even walks in the park are hard because I’m always scanning the ground, terrified one will drop from a tree.

At first, I thought it would pass, but it’s only gotten stronger. I know it sounds irrational—my daughter says it’s just a bug, and logically I get that—but I can’t control it. The fear takes over. I avoid anything where I might see one. Work’s getting harder too—we had a pest issue last month, and I nearly had a breakdown. I just want to feel normal again.
D012_m011.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D012_m012.question:
I’ve been like this for over two years now—almost two and a half, actually—and it’s gotten harder to ignore. Ever since I took my son to that big kids’ birthday party with the clown, something just clicked in the wrong way. I can’t explain it, but the moment I saw that guy in the costume—painted face, goofy wig, the whole thing—I froze. My heart started racing, I couldn’t breathe right, and I had to get out fast. Since then, I just avoid anything like that. Parades, circuses, even cartoons with exaggerated faces on TV… just the thought makes my skin crawl.

I know it sounds irrational—my husband says I’m overreacting—but I can’t help it. The fear feels real. I won’t go to events if there’s even a chance there might be a costume. If I *have* to go somewhere, I make my husband come with me. Just knowing he’s there, that he’ll step in or get me out if something happens, is the only thing that keeps me from completely falling apart. Without him? I don’t think I could do it. Even driving past a store with a mascot out front makes me swerve onto a different street. It’s exhausting, honestly—always watching for triggers, always on edge.
D012_m012.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D012_m013.question:
I’ve been a nurse for about five years now, and honestly, work has been really hard lately—not because of the patients, but because of me. It started a couple years ago, maybe two years and a little over a month now, when I was helping with a feeding tube insertion. The patient coughed, and something about the sound—this deep, gagging noise—just terrified me. Ever since then, I can't stop thinking about choking. Not even my own—mostly that someone will choke in front of me, and I won’t be able to help. But sometimes I get this wave of panic thinking I might choke on food too.

I don’t go out to eat with friends anymore. Even packing a lunch at home makes me anxious. I avoid certain textures—anything sticky or chunky—and I’ve stopped working certain shifts in the ER because they sometimes bring in code blues with airway issues. I tell them I’m not feeling well. The truth is, I just can’t handle it. I even skip birthday parties because of cake and candles. It sounds silly, but the fear feels real. It’s like my body takes over—heart racing, shaky, can’t breathe—just thinking about it. And the more it happens, the more I stay away.
D012_m013.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D012_m014.question:
I’ve been struggling with this for over two years now—since right after my daughter was born, actually. It started when we visited my wife’s family in another city and I had to take a train through a long tunnel. I freaked out—heart racing, couldn’t breathe, felt like I was going to pass out. Since then, I’ve been avoiding anything like that: tunnels, tall bridges, even elevators.  

As a chef, it’s starting to mess with my work. We got invited to a big industry event in the city, but it’s on the 15th floor of a building. I told my wife I’d go, but when it came time to get in the elevator, I just couldn’t. I took the stairs both ways—and it made me so late that I missed my panel. She ended up coming with me last time we flew, and that’s the only way I made it through security without panicking. Just knowing she’s there helps. If she’s not around, I’ll make up excuses—say I’m sick or stuck at the restaurant.  

I know it sounds crazy. Nothing’s happened, and logically I know I’m safe. But when I think about being trapped like that, my chest tightens and I feel like I’m losing control. I just want it to stop—I miss traveling with my family, doing my job without fear.
D012_m014.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D012_m015.question:
I’ve been having this problem for about two years now—just over two years, actually—where the sight of blood or even thinking about needles or medical stuff just completely shuts me down. It’s gotten so bad that I’ll feel dizzy, like I’m going to pass out, my vision tunnels, and my heart races… but then suddenly it feels like everything’s slowing down. I’ve actually fainted a couple times, just from seeing a deep cut on a coworker during a call. 

I know it sounds bad, especially in my job. I’m a firefighter—part of a rescue team—and we see trauma all the time. But lately, I’ve been asking to hang back when there’s visible injury, or I’ll redirect to equipment duty. My crew’s noticed. My wife’s worried too. I skipped my last check-up and haven’t had any vaccines because I can’t handle the needle. I even almost quit when they required a routine blood draw. 

I don’t want to let my team down, but just the thought of it… I can’t. It’s like my body takes over and I have no control. I avoid anything medical—no hospitals, no donating blood, nothing. I just can’t risk blacking out, especially when people are counting on me.
D012_m015.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D012_m016.question:
I’ve had this thing with spiders for about a year and a half now—doesn’t make sense, I know, especially since I carry a gun for a living. But when I see one, even a tiny spider, my chest locks up, my heart starts hammering like it’s trying to get out, and I can’t breathe right. It’s instant—doesn’t matter if it’s in the precinct bathroom or in my apartment. I freeze. Last month, I had to clear a storage room during a call, and there was this little house spider in the corner? I couldn't do it. Had to ask the rookie to go in instead. Made no sense to him. Makes no sense to me.

I don’t go anywhere in the garage or basement alone. If I have to, I bring my flashlight—the one with the bright beam—and I keep checking the floor, walls, ceiling. I’ve started leaving lights on all night at home. If I’m with someone I trust, I can handle it a little better—just knowing they’re there helps. But it’s getting worse. I turned down an indoor search warrant because it was an old building—dusty, dark. I didn’t want to see what was in the corners. I can’t keep doing that on the job. It’s not safe. It’s not like me.
D012_m016.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)

D012_m017.question:
I’ve always been into crypto trading—work from anywhere, set my own hours—but this thing with storms has pretty much taken over my life. It started about a year and a half ago after I got caught in this insane thunderstorm while I was hiking. Since then, any sign of bad weather just… shuts me down. I mean, the second the sky darkens or I hear thunder, I can’t move. My chest locks up, my legs feel like stone—I just freeze, even if I’m just looking out a window. I know it sounds irrational, but I can’t help it.

Now, I check weather apps constantly. If there’s even a 30% chance of rain, I won’t leave my apartment. That’s made things tough—missed a few key trading calls because I wouldn’t go to a co-working space, and I stopped traveling altogether. I had to back out of a friend’s wedding in Miami because of hurricane season. I live in a high-rise, so I tell myself I’m safe up here, but even then, when the wind hits a certain pitch, I crawl into a corner and just wait it out. It’s embarrassing, honestly. But what if something happens and I can’t get out? I can’t trade when I’m like that. I just freeze.
D012_m017.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)

D012_m018.question:
I’ve been struggling with this for about a year and a half now, and honestly, it’s starting to feel ridiculous. I’m a fund manager—I handle high-pressure calls, multi-million-dollar decisions, all that. But lately, I’ve been avoiding team lunches, client dinners, even my son’s birthday party because… I can’t stand the sound of balloons popping. It’s not just that I don’t like it—it’s full-on terror. 

When I hear that noise, or even think about it, my heart slams like it’s trying to get out of my chest. I can’t breathe, I start sweating, my hands shake—it feels like I’m having a heart attack. My wife doesn’t get it. Last week, she brought home decorations for our nephew’s party. Just seeing an inflated balloon in the living room made me bolt to the bedroom. I locked the door. I know how that looks.

I’ve started mapping out every event, every party, to make sure there won’t be balloons. I’ve declined weddings, missed my cousin’s baby shower. It’s affecting my relationships, and I feel like I’m losing control. The worst part? I can’t explain why it’s balloons. I just know that if I hear one pop, I won’t be able to handle it.
D012_m018.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)

D012_m019.question:
I’ve been struggling with this for about a year and a half now, and it’s starting to really affect my work. As a real estate agent, I’m constantly having to meet clients, show apartments, and travel across the city—and that usually means taking elevators, especially in high-rises. But lately, just the thought of stepping into one makes my chest tighten. My heart starts racing, I get sweaty, and it feels like I can’t catch my breath, even if it’s just two floors. 

I’ve started refusing listings in buildings without stairs, which is embarrassing when clients ask why. I took the stairs up to a 12th-floor condo once—arrived completely out of breath and late. My husband thinks I’m overreacting, but it’s not like I don’t want to go in; I just *can’t*. I’ve even driven an extra 20 minutes to avoid the highway tunnel. Last week, I declined a potential buyer because they wanted to see a penthouse unit—automatic elevator. 

I know it doesn’t make sense, but the fear feels physical, like something awful will happen the moment the doors close. I’m worried I’m going to lose clients—or worse, my career—if I can’t get past this.
D012_m019.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)

D012_m020.question: I’ve been driving a cab for over twenty years, so I’m on the road all day, every day. About a year and a half ago, I started getting this real tightness in my chest whenever I had to go through tunnels—especially the long one near the river. At first, I thought it was just my heart, maybe stress, but it kept happening. Now, even thinking about approaching one gets me worked up—the palms sweat, heart races, like I can’t breathe. I’ve started taking longer routes, adding miles I don’t need, just to avoid them. But sometimes, there’s no way around it—traffic forces me in, or a passenger needs to get through quick. When that happens, I white-knuckle the wheel, try to focus on the radio, keep telling myself “you’re fine, just drive,” but it’s terrifying. I feel like I’m going to pass out or crash. My ex-wife said I should see someone, but I’ve always handled things on my own. Lately, though, it’s messing with my work. I lose time going out of the way, and when I can’t avoid the tunnel, I’m shook for the rest of the shift. It’s getting hard to ignore.
D012_m020.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)

D012_m021.question:
I’ve been dreading this for a while, but I finally had to make this appointment. For the past year, I’ve been having these overwhelming waves of panic whenever I have to get on an airplane or go into enclosed spaces—especially elevators. I’m a bankruptcy lawyer, so my job means I travel between courts, client meetings, sometimes out of state. I can’t just avoid it, no matter how much I want to.

I remember last month, I had to go to a hearing in another city. I drove eight hours instead of flying because the thought of boarding a plane makes my chest tighten, my hands sweat—like I can’t breathe. And when I get in an elevator, even just going up three floors at my office building, I feel trapped. I keep telling myself, “It’s okay, it’s safe,” but my body doesn’t listen. My heart races, I feel dizzy, and I’m convinced something terrible is going to happen.

I’ve tried to push through—I have no choice with my job—but every time, it leaves me shaken for hours. I’m single, so there’s no one really checking in on me, and I’m starting to feel embarrassed. This isn’t me. I’m supposed to be composed, in control. But lately, I’m terrified of the next situation I can’t avoid.
D012_m021.options:
A. Specific Phobia
    B. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Generalized Anxiety Disorder

D012_m022.question:
I’ve been having this really intense fear of loud, sudden sounds—like explosions or thunder or even loud sound effects in movies. It’s been going on for about a year now, and honestly, it’s messed with my head more than I’d like to admit. I know it sounds weird, especially since I’m a pro gamer—some of the games we play have loud in-game sounds, and tournaments have big crowds and pyrotechnics. But when those noises hit, my chest tightens, my heart races, and I feel like I can’t breathe. I start sweating and just want to get out. Fast.

I’ve tried to push through it because I can’t exactly quit tournaments or avoid game trailers. Last month at a live event, they had fireworks during the opening, and I just froze. Had to sit down, felt like I was losing control. I didn’t want anyone to notice, so I didn’t say anything, but inside, I was screaming. It’s exhausting, pretending you’re fine when every nerve is on fire. I don’t know why I react this way—it’s not like anything bad ever happened. But the fear feels so real, like something terrible is about to happen every time.
D012_m022.options:
A. Specific Phobia
    B. Major Depressive Disorder with Psychotic Features
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Generalized Anxiety Disorder

D012_m023.question:
I’ve been avoiding certain places and situations for about a year now, and it’s starting to affect my work and my son’s life too. I represent a local dealership, so I’m usually out at community events—car shows, charity drives, stuff like that. But anytime there’s a mascot or someone in a costume, like at a kid’s event, I get this sudden rush of panic. My heart slams, I can’t catch my breath, and I just know something awful is going to happen. It’s not just discomfort—it’s full-blown terror.

I’ve started refusing invitations unless I know there won’t be any costumed characters. When I have to go, I only show up if my assistant comes with me. Just knowing he’s nearby helps a little—he’s like a grounding wire. I don’t know why this started, but it’s gotten worse. I don’t understand why this happened. I used to be fine. Now, I rearrange my life just to avoid these situations, and even when I force myself, I feel like I might pass out. It’s exhausting.

A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Generalized Anxiety Disorder

D012_m047.question:
I’m a corporate lawyer, and I’ve been married for eight years—we have a five-year-old daughter. My job is demanding, but I can handle the stress. What I can’t handle is flying. It’s been like this for over a year now—maybe a year and four months. It started after a turbulent flight back from a deposition in Denver, and since then, just thinking about boarding a plane makes my chest tighten.

I don’t mind the airports or even the idea of travel—just the moment the plane doors close and we start taxiing. My heart races, I feel dizzy, like I can’t breathe. Once, on a work trip, I had to go—I didn’t have a choice—but I sat there gripping the armrests the whole time, sweating, convinced something would go wrong. I kept thinking about storms, about the plane losing altitude, even though I know it’s irrational.  

I’ve started turning down cases that require travel. I make excuses, say I’ll handle things remotely. My husband doesn’t understand—he thinks I’ve just become “risk-averse.” But it’s not about control or logic; it’s pure fear. I endure it when I absolutely must, but it’s miserable.
D012_m047.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Generalized Anxiety Disorder

D012_m048.question:
I’ve been driving a taxi for over fifteen years—know every backroad and shortcut in this city. Since my divorce two years back, it’s just me and the cab, really. But for the past year and a half, something’s gotten worse: I can’t stop thinking about spiders. Not even big ones—just the thought of seeing one, anywhere, makes my chest tighten. I know it sounds silly—a grown man scared of bugs—but it’s not just seeing them. Just *imagining* one crawling in the car, under the seat, or worse, on my arm while I’m driving… it’s enough to make me break into a sweat.

I’ve started checking the backseat and floor with a flashlight before every shift. If a passenger’s been riding with groceries or luggage from outside, I get anxious—what if something hitched a ride? Last winter, I turned down a fare near that old warehouse district because the place is grimy, lots of cobwebs. Lost good money, but I just couldn’t risk it. Now I stick to the clean, busy routes. My dispatcher’s noticed. Said I’m “picky.” Truth is, I’m just trying not to lose it in the middle of a ride.

A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Generalized Anxiety Disorder

D012_m049.question:
I’ve been the head librarian here for over twenty years—routine and quiet have always been part of the job, and honestly, part of what I’ve always appreciated. But for the past year and a bit, I’ve had this… well, it sounds absurd, I know, but I can’t stand storytime anymore. That’s when the children come in with their parents, and some of them wear those full costumes—silly animal suits or superhero outfits. The moment one of those characters walks in, my chest tightens. My heart starts racing like I’m being chased, even though I know rationally nothing’s wrong. I break into a sweat, and sometimes I feel like I can’t catch my breath.

I’ve tried to avoid it—letting my assistant lead storytime—but it’s my responsibility. So I stay. I stand in the back, gripping the book cart, trembling, counting the minutes until it’s over. It’s humiliating at my age, my position, to feel so overwhelmed by something so childish. But the fear doesn’t care about logic. It’s been happening nearly every week for over a year now, and it’s starting to affect how I feel just coming into work.
D012_m049.options:
A. Acute Stress Disorder
    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Generalized Anxiety Disorder

D012_m050.question:
I’ve always been the kind of person who likes control—running a business, keeping things on track, staying ahead. But for the past year and a half, I’ve been dealing with something I just can’t seem to manage, and it’s starting to affect everything. Anytime a storm rolls in, I completely shut down. I mean, I *freeze*. My chest tightens, I can’t breathe right, my legs won’t move—I just stand there like I’m glued to the floor. Once, during a thunderstorm, I couldn’t even get out of my office to drive home. I ended up staying overnight because the idea of driving in the rain felt impossible.

I know it sounds irrational, but the sky darkening or that first clap of thunder—it’s like a switch flips. I’ve started checking weather reports obsessively. If there’s even a 30% chance of rain, I reschedule meetings, cancel dinners, or work from home. I’ve turned down business trips, avoided industry events—my wife’s noticed, my employees have noticed. I’ve always been dependable, but now I feel like I’m letting people down… and I’m terrified of the next storm rolling in.

    B. Specific Phobia
    C. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    D. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
